To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
MAPs reduce MT dynamic behavior, that MAP‐free MT dynamic behavior can be restored by MAP removal, and that MAP‐2 second repeat peptides can also reduce MT dynamic behavior.
MAPs can reduce the dynamic instability of microtubules and that a peptide analogue of the second repeated sequence of MAP‐2 is capable of mimicking the effect of intact MAPs.

MAP‐2 can modulate MT dynamics, that MAP‐2 binding to MTs can be reduced by a peptide analogue, and that the MAP‐2 second repeated sequence analogue is sufficient to mimic the effects of MAP‐2 on MT dynamics.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of brain MAPs in the control of MT assembly and dynamics and the ability of MAP‐2 second repeated sequence peptides to mimic the action of MAPs.
understanding the role of MAPs in MT length regulation and the mechanisms by which they can modulate MT dynamics.
the regulation of microtubule assembly and disassembly by microtubule-associated proteins (MAPs).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
MAPs are able to modulate the dynamic instability of MTs.
MAPs and MAP‐2 peptide analogues can retard MT dynamic instability.

MAPs can influence MT dynamics by two distinct and independent mechanisms: one involving the ability of MAPs to bind to MTs, and the other involving the ability of some MAPs to promote tubulin assembly in the absence of MTs.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a single peptide sequence in the MT binding region of MAP‐1 or MAP‐2 can modulate MT dynamics, and that MAP‐1 and MAP‐2 may be able to regulate MT dynamics in a similar manner.
MAP‐binding peptides can modulate MT polymerization dynamics in vitro and that MAPs can regulate the rates of MT assembly/disassembly in cells.
MAPs, and at least the MAP‐2 second repeat, can influence MT assembly and disassembly dynamics in vitro.
The main takeaway from our work is that
microtubules are dynamic structures that can change their length by polymerization and depolymerization.
the dynamic behavior of microtubules can be regulated in vitro by the addition of brain microtubule‐binding proteins (MAPs) or by a MAP‐2 second repeated sequence peptide analogue.
the dynamic instability model can be used to describe the effects of MAPs on MT dynamics.
